By various accounts I've stumbled across in the last hour or two, musl is an implementation of libc that aims to be more performant, less bloated, and more robust than glibc. Sounds appealing! glibc is running in basically everything on the system, if not statically linked, then dynamically linked. Bloat in this package is bad news for your CPU's instruction cache.

One consumer of musl is Alpine Linux which has a litany of compelling features (mainly security and efficiency. And, needless to say, no systemd.)

Meanwhile, Gentoo (which I'm using now) apparently has an overlay for anyone who wants to switch, which is probably better than installing a new OS. And of course, the means of hardening Gentoo are also well documented, and are perhaps as good as Alpine, modulo the leg work?

The only thing Gentoo doesn't do is run entirely in RAM... but doesn't virtual memory tend to obviate that? Wouldn't upgrading to an SSD have nearly the same effect? I load URXVT first thing in the morning, and it's slow to load because it's not in memory yet. After that, it's pretty snappy and presumably never leaves memory.

...Now I'm thinking I should take advantage of what's already here instead of jumping ship.
Why the fuck am I not using AlpineLinux?

A point I should iterate on. Switching to an SSD will not equal the OS running in RAM. An SSD is still orders of magnitude slower than ram. An SSD is a great performance boost, and you will notice at at times such as boot, and loading an unloaded application. If you are still running spinning rust for your data transactions, you are going to feel as if the machine is ridiculously faster.
No systemd is a deal-breaker for me. Also, why BusyBox? I get going for space efficiency, but BusyBox is quite neutered compared to the traditional tools.

It makes admining my Arch systems much easier. I have six in total, one of which is my router, and it's nice how everything just works right out of the box. When I have an issue, usually with a network interface during initial setup, the journal lets me know pretty fast what went wrong. I really wish we had systemd at work too for the timers, but that probably won't happen for a few more years. Cron is a mess, and we make extensive use of it.
Gotcha. Is that benefit really with the security risk though?

Filesystem cache alleviate nearly any performance advantage to running something in a ram disk. This is a reason I suggest getting a c programming book for linux. It makes you learn how the system works. Really your files live in RAM with a disk persistence layer. They are dynamically loaded into RAM and this selection essentially supports sharding.

If you wanted you could make a ram disk and then you could write something in fuse to identify changes and copy them over to a disk version of the same drive. Essentially what you would end up with is exactly what you already have plus the limitation of your ram size.

Running stuff in RAM is for when you want to hide things and you never want it to touch disk. You should just use encryption for that though.
